title: 'Exosomes and Extracellular Vesicles: Signals Between Cells'

generated.pipeline: extract → Gemini draft → Claude Sonnet accuracy gate → Sonnet fixes

cards.front: {{c1::Extracellular vesicles}} are small membrane sacs released into surrounding fluid, carrying surface membrane proteins and internal cytosolic protein and RNA.
cards.quote: Extracellular vesicles are small membrane sacs released into surrounding fluid.
cards.section: Vesicles can carry a signal: the clearest case

cards.front: What three experimental tasks are required to prove extracellular vesicle signalling?
cards.back: Separating the vesicles from other material, locating the cargo (surface versus lumen), and counting cargo copies relative to particles.
cards.why: Proving a vesicle signalling claim also requires mock, dose, and specificity controls.
cards.quote: Extracellular vesicles keep cell orientation: ligands face out, internal cargo stays sealed; proving vesicle signalling requires separating vesicles, locating cargo, and counting copies.
cards.section: Vesicles can carry a signal: the clearest case

cards.front: Vesicles released by B cells carrying peptide-loaded MHC class II stimulate only T cells whose receptor recognises that exact peptide on that MHC molecule. What does this specificity establish?
cards.back: It establishes that the vesicle's surface peptide–MHC complex itself delivered the signal, acting like an antigen-presenting cell without anything entering the T cell.
cards.why: A stray soluble growth factor co-pelleted with the vesicles could not distinguish between matching and non-matching T-cell receptors.
cards.quote: Added to cultured T cells, the vesicles stimulated only T cells whose receptor recognised that exact peptide on that MHC molecule.
cards.section: Vesicles can carry a signal: the clearest case

cards.front: An {{c1::exosome}} is a single-membrane vesicle that forms inside a multivesicular body and is released when that compartment fuses with the plasma membrane.
cards.back: Usually quoted as about 30 to 100 nanometres across, too small to resolve in a light microscope.
cards.quote: Fusing with a lysosome digests the internal vesicles; moving to the surface and fusing with the plasma membrane releases them intact as exosomes.
cards.section: Where the vesicles come from: one compartment, two exits

cards.front: What are the two possible exit fates of a multivesicular body inside a cell?
cards.back: It can fuse with a lysosome to digest its internal vesicles, or fuse with the plasma membrane to release them intact as exosomes.
cards.quote: The compartment is a sorting room with two doors: one to the incinerator and one to the street.
cards.section: Where the vesicles come from: one compartment, two exits

cards.front: Why does a plasma-membrane receptor keep its ligand-binding domain facing outward on an exosome even though exosomes form inside an endosome?
cards.back: Two membrane inversions cancel out: endocytosis turns the domain inward into the endosome, and inward budding away from the cytosol flips it back outward while sealing cytosol inside.
cards.quote: Pushing cytosol into each bud flips the membrane back: the ligand-binding domain again faces outward, and cytosol is sealed inside.
cards.section: Where the vesicles come from: one compartment, two exits

cards.front: How does a microvesicle (ectosome) differ in origin from an exosome, and why do both share the same membrane orientation?
cards.back: A microvesicle buds straight outward from the plasma membrane, skipping the endosome. Both bud away from the cytosol (zero versus two inversions), keeping ectodomains outside and cytosol inside.
cards.quote: That bud also forms away from the cytosol, with zero inversions instead of two, so a microvesicle has the same orientation as an exosome.
cards.section: Where the vesicles come from: one compartment, two exits

cards.front: You treat a mixed preparation of exosomes and microvesicles with a protease (without detergent) to try to tell them apart. What happens, and why?
cards.back: The test cannot distinguish them. Both vesicle types carry ectodomains outside and cytosol inside, so protease cuts the same surface proteins and spares the same lumenal ones on both.
cards.why: Distinguishing exosomes from microvesicles requires evidence of origin, such as images of a multivesicular body fusing with the plasma membrane.
cards.quote: Both kinds carry their ectodomains outside and cytosol inside, so a protease cuts the same surface proteins on both and spares the same lumenal ones.
cards.section: Where the vesicles come from: one compartment, two exits

cards.front: A plasma-membrane receptor has its ligand-binding domain outside the cell and its tail in the cytosol. After endocytosis and inward budding into a multivesicular body, where do those two ends face inside the multivesicular body and after exosome release?
cards.back: In both states, the ligand-binding domain faces outside the small vesicle (first into the multivesicular-body fluid, then into extracellular fluid) and the tail remains inside the vesicle lumen with trapped cytosol.
cards.why: Inward budding restores cell orientation inside the multivesicular body, and fusion with the plasma membrane releases the intact vesicle without inverting it again.
cards.quote: Plasma membrane pinches inward to form an endosome, turning the receptor's ligand-binding domain inward into the endosome fluid while its tail stays in the cytosol.
cards.section: Where the vesicles come from: one compartment, two exits

cards.front: A drug blocks fusion of multivesicular bodies with the plasma membrane without affecting outward budding from the plasma membrane. Predict how exosome release, microvesicle release, and the orientation of remaining released vesicles change, and why.
cards.back: Exosome release stops while microvesicle release continues, and the surface orientation of released vesicles stays unchanged. By the two-exit and membrane-inversion rules, blocking plasma-membrane fusion prevents multivesicular bodies from releasing exosomes, whereas microvesicles bud straight outward away from the cytosol with the same right-side-out orientation.
cards.quote: Microvesicles (or ectosomes) bud straight outward from the plasma membrane, skipping the endosome.
cards.section: Where the vesicles come from: one compartment, two exits

cards.front: Tetraspanins such as {{c1::CD9, CD63 and CD81}} are membrane proteins with four membrane-spanning helices shared by both exosomes and microvesicles.
cards.quote: tetraspanins such as CD9, CD63 and CD81, membrane proteins with four membrane-spanning helices
cards.section: Where the vesicles come from: one compartment, two exits

cards.front: Why does the International Society for Extracellular Vesicles (ISEV) urge calling isolated vesicles "extracellular vesicles" rather than "exosomes" unless origin is proved?
cards.back: Exosomes and microvesicles share membrane orientation, size range, and common markers such as tetraspanins, so no agreed test reliably separates them once mixed in medium.
cards.quote: The International Society for Extracellular Vesicles (ISEV) therefore urges "extracellular vesicle" or "small extracellular vesicle" unless origin is proved.
cards.section: Where the vesicles come from: one compartment, two exits

cards.front: How do synaptic vesicles differ fundamentally from extracellular vesicles?
cards.back: Synaptic vesicles remain inside neurons, fuse with the plasma membrane to release soluble transmitter, and are recycled rather than released intact into surrounding fluid.
cards.quote: Synaptic vesicles differ completely: they remain inside neurons, fuse to release soluble transmitter, and are recycled.
cards.section: Where the vesicles come from: one compartment, two exits

cards.front: Inward budding into a multivesicular body typically uses {{c1::ESCRT}} protein complexes with partners such as ALIX, although alternative routes such as a ceramide-dependent pathway also exist.
cards.quote: Inward budding uses ESCRT protein complexes with partners such as ALIX; alternative routes exist (one depending on the lipid ceramide)
cards.section: Where the vesicles come from: one compartment, two exits

cards.front: What four classes of molecules can an extracellular vesicle carry by geometry?
cards.back: Membrane proteins (including receptors), cytosolic proteins, membrane lipids, and RNA.
cards.quote: By geometry, vesicles carry membrane proteins (including receptors), cytosolic proteins, membrane lipids and RNA.
cards.section: What is inside, and three ways it could act

cards.front: Carefully purified small extracellular vesicles contain mostly {{c1::transfer RNA}} and other small non-coding RNAs, with far less than one copy of any given microRNA per vesicle on average.
cards.quote: Yet carefully purified small vesicles hold mostly transfer RNA and other small non-coding RNAs
cards.section: What is inside, and three ways it could act

cards.front: Why does sphere geometry impose a low copy-number ceiling on unenriched cytosolic cargo inside a 100 nanometre extracellular vesicle?
cards.back: A 100 nanometre sphere holds at most about 5 × 10^-19 litres (less inside its bilayer), so at 1 micromolar passive trapping captures only about 0.3 molecules per vesicle.
cards.quote: At 1 micromolar in cytosol, passive trapping captures only about 0.3 molecules per vesicle unless cargo is concentrated.
cards.section: What is inside, and three ways it could act

cards.front: A 100 nanometre sphere encloses at most about 5 × 10^-19 litres and passively traps about 0.3 cytosolic molecules at 1 micromolar. For a 50 nanometre exosome at 1 micromolar, by what factor does sphere volume drop, and roughly how many molecules are trapped on average?
cards.back: Sphere volume scales with diameter cubed, so halving diameter cuts volume 2^3 = 8-fold (to about 6 × 10^-20 litres). The passive average drops eightfold: 0.3 ÷ 8 ≈ 0.04 molecules per vesicle (less inside the bilayer).
cards.quote: Volume scales with diameter cubed, so halving diameter cuts volume eightfold ($2^3 = 8$), dropping the passive average from about 0.3 to roughly 0.04 molecules per vesicle
cards.section: What is inside, and three ways it could act

cards.front: A 100 nanometre vesicle passively traps about 0.3 molecules per vesicle of a cytosolic solute present at 1 micromolar. Without active concentration, roughly what cytosolic concentration is needed to passively average 3 molecules per 100 nanometre vesicle?
cards.back: About 10 micromolar. At fixed vesicle volume, passively trapped molecules scale linearly with concentration: (3 ÷ 0.3) × 1 micromolar = 10 micromolar (and somewhat higher once the bilayer thickness reduces inner volume).
cards.quote: A 100 nanometre sphere encloses at most about $5 \times 10^{-19}$ litres (less inside its bilayer).
cards.section: What is inside, and three ways it could act

cards.front: What are the three main ways an extracellular vesicle could act on a target cell?
cards.back: Surface-ligand binding to a target receptor, membrane fusion releasing internal cargo into the cytosol, or endocytic uptake (which signals only if cargo is sensed en route or escapes).
cards.quote: A vesicle could therefore act in three ways, each requiring different evidence: Surface ligand.
cards.section: What is inside, and three ways it could act

cards.front: A lab labels purified extracellular vesicles with a fluorescent dye, adds them to cultured cells, and sees bright fluorescent dots inside the cells. Can they conclude that vesicle RNA reached the cytosol? Why or why not?
cards.back: No. Intracellular fluorescent dots show endocytic uptake, not cytosolic release. Swallowed vesicles usually traffic to the lysosome unless their cargo escapes or is sensed along the way.
cards.quote: Uptake alone proves little, because swallowed material usually reaches the lysosome; it signals only if cargo is sensed on the way or escapes.
cards.section: What is inside, and three ways it could act

cards.front: Purified 100 nanometre vesicles carry many copies of a surface receptor ligand and passively trap an unenriched cytosolic enzyme present at 1 micromolar in donor cells. If a low vesicle dose triggers a strong response in recipient cells, which signalling route is much better supported, and why?
cards.back: Surface-ligand signalling is much better supported. By the sphere-volume and delivery-barrier rules, passive trapping at 1 micromolar captures only about 0.3 enzyme copies per vesicle and lumenal cargo must still cross a membrane to reach the cytosol, whereas outer-surface ligands can be present at many copies and signal without crossing a bilayer.
cards.quote: Meanwhile, a vesicle's outer surface can display many copies of a membrane protein without anything crossing a bilayer.
cards.section: What is inside, and three ways it could act

cards.front: What are the three sequential spin steps in standard differential ultracentrifugation to pellet small extracellular vesicles?
cards.back: A slow spin clears cells and debris, a faster spin removes large vesicles, and about 100,000 times gravity for an hour or more pellets small vesicles.
cards.quote: a slow spin clears cells and debris, a faster spin removes large vesicles, and about 100,000 times gravity for an hour or more pellets small vesicles.
cards.section: How would you know? The pellet is defined by the centrifuge

cards.front: Why does biological activity in a 100,000 × g pellet not by itself prove that extracellular vesicles carried the signal?
cards.back: High-speed spinning co-pellets anything of similar size and density, including protein aggregates, lipoproteins, RNA–protein complexes, viruses, calf-serum vesicles, and stuck soluble growth factors.
cards.quote: Everything of similar size and density sediments too: protein aggregates, lipoproteins, RNA–protein complexes, viruses, vesicles from calf serum in the medium, and stuck soluble growth factors.
cards.section: How would you know? The pellet is defined by the centrifuge

cards.front: When Robert Coffey's laboratory separated ultracentrifuge pellets on density gradients and independently captured vesicles with antibodies without high-speed spinning, what did they find regarding Argonaute proteins and DNA?
cards.back: Argonaute proteins (which carry microRNA) were not detected in exosomes, and small vesicles were not vehicles of active DNA release.
cards.why: Contaminants co-pelleted by high-speed spinning alone had previously distorted conclusions about exosome cargo.
cards.quote: Argonaute proteins (which carry microRNA) were not detected in exosomes, and small vesicles were not vehicles of active DNA release.
cards.section: How would you know? The pellet is defined by the centrifuge

cards.front: A 100,000 × g pellet increases proliferation of target cells. Bottom-loaded on a sucrose density gradient and spun to equilibrium, fractions at 1.13–1.19 g/mL hold 85% of the membrane markers and 8% of the activity, while denser fractions below hold no marker and 82% of the activity. What does this show?
cards.back: Most of the activity is carried by something denser than small vesicles, such as free or aggregated protein, rather than the vesicles themselves.
cards.why: Small vesicles in sucrose float to about 1.13–1.19 g/mL with membrane markers, whereas free protein and dense aggregates stay below.
cards.quote: Small vesicles in sucrose usually rise to about 1.13–1.19 g/mL and free protein stays below; activity should float with the membrane markers
cards.section: How would you know? The pellet is defined by the centrifuge

cards.front: After spinning conditioned culture medium at 100,000 × g to pellet small vesicles, you test the post-spin supernatant on recipient cells and find it reproduces the pellet's full biological activity. What does this indicate, and why?
cards.back: A soluble factor (or serum component), rather than pelleted vesicles, likely drives the activity. Small vesicles sediment into the 100,000 × g pellet, so a true vesicle signal should not be reproduced by the post-spin supernatant.
cards.quote: Neither reproduces the pellet's activity (even vesicle-depleted serum keeps much of its RNA)
cards.section: How would you know? The pellet is defined by the centrifuge

cards.front: Density-purified vesicles carrying protein Y and a lumenal control protein are split three ways for western blotting. Untreated: both are present. Protease alone: Y vanishes while the lumenal control stays intact. Protease plus detergent: both vanish. Where is Y, and how could it signal most directly?
cards.back: Protein Y is on the outer vesicle surface (or loosely bound outside), so it could bind a surface receptor on a target cell without entering.
cards.why: Survival of the lumenal control confirms intact membranes blocked protease from entering; detergent was needed to expose lumenal cargo.
cards.quote: Lumenal cargo survives enzyme alone and vanishes only with detergent
cards.section: How would you know? The pellet is defined by the centrifuge

cards.front: Why can an RNA species survive RNase treatment without detergent even if it is actually outside sealed vesicles?
cards.back: RNA-binding proteins such as Argonaute can shield loose, non-vesicular RNA from RNase digestion, mimicking protection inside a vesicle lumen.
cards.quote: bound proteins like Argonaute can shield loose RNA from RNase
cards.section: How would you know? The pellet is defined by the centrifuge

cards.front: To check stoichiometry in a vesicle preparation, calculate copies per vesicle = {{c1::copies of the cargo measured ÷ particles counted}}.
cards.back: A ratio far below one weakens a signalling claim unless a rare vesicle subset carries most copies.
cards.quote: copies per vesicle = copies of the cargo measured ÷ particles counted
cards.section: How would you know? The pellet is defined by the centrifuge

cards.front: A density-purified vesicle preparation has 4 × 10^10 counted particles and 2 × 10^9 measured copies of a microRNA. RNase alone removes 80% of the RNA signal, while RNase plus detergent removes 100%. What is the protected copies-per-vesicle ratio, and by what factor did the untreated ratio overstate it?
cards.back: 0.01 protected copies per vesicle (1 copy per 100 vesicles), overstated fivefold before RNase. Only 20% survives RNase alone (0.20 × 2 × 10^9 = 4 × 10^8 lumenal copies); 4 × 10^8 ÷ 4 × 10^10 = 0.01, versus 0.05 untreated (0.05 ÷ 0.01 = 5).
cards.quote: Most of it was outside sealed vesicles, loose or stuck to their surface, because RNase without detergent cannot reach lumenal cargo.
cards.section: How would you know? The pellet is defined by the centrifuge

cards.front: You spin medium from donor cells A, add the pellet to recipient cells B, and B changes behaviour. What control experiment rules out calf serum in the medium as the source of the activity?
cards.back: Grow cells A without serum (or in vesicle-depleted serum) and test a mock pellet spun from cell-free medium. If the mock pellet reproduces the effect, the medium—not cells A—caused it.
cards.why: Calf serum brings its own vesicles and growth factors, and even vesicle-depleted serum retains much of its RNA.
cards.quote: Grow A without serum, or in vesicle-depleted serum (a long spin still leaves much serum RNA behind), and test a mock pellet from cell-free medium.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: When recipient cells B are immune cells that respond to a vesicle pellet from cells A, what bacterial contaminant can mimic a vesicle signal, and how do you rule it out?
cards.back: Trace bacterial lipopolysaccharide (LPS) can switch on Toll-like receptor 4. Rule it out by assaying the pellet for lipopolysaccharide and repeating the test on recipient cells lacking Toll-like receptor 4.
cards.quote: If B is an immune cell, trace bacterial lipopolysaccharide switches on Toll-like receptor 4. Assay for lipopolysaccharide and repeat with B cells lacking that receptor.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Deleting the gene for candidate cargo X in donor cells A abolishes the ability of A's vesicle pellet to alter recipient cells B. Before concluding that cargo X carried the vesicle signal, what donor-cell pitfall and dose check must you address?
cards.back: Based on cargo-specificity and realistic-dose rules, check whether deleting the gene altered donor cells A themselves or changed their other vesicles, and verify that the active particle dose matches A's release rate and holds under titration.
cards.quote: A pellet from A cells lacking the candidate cargo should fail—checking also whether deleting the gene altered A or its other vesicles.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Suppose serum-mock, density-gradient, contaminant, dose-titration, and cargo-knockout controls all confirm that vesicles from cells A signal to cells B. Why can you still not call the active particles "exosomes"?
cards.back: By the origin-definition and control rules, those assays prove extracellular-vesicle signalling but not biogenesis. Calling the particles exosomes also requires proving multivesicular-body origin rather than outward plasma-membrane budding.
cards.quote: With all four done you have a strong case for vesicle signalling from A. To call them exosomes, you must also prove multivesicular-body origin.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Why is reticulocyte transferrin-receptor shedding a well-established role for exosomes even though it demonstrates no intercellular message?
cards.back: Maturing red blood cells discard transferrin receptors they no longer need for iron import, so exosome release functions cleanly as protein disposal without requiring any target-cell signal.
cards.quote: Disposal. Reticulocyte transferrin-receptor shedding stands cleanly without needing any message.
cards.section: Where the evidence is good, and where it is argued

cards.front: Why is Schwann-cell vesicle promotion of sensory-axon regrowth classified as supported rather than closed?
cards.back: The evidence rests on adding prepared vesicles to cultured axons and injured nerves rather than proving the full endogenous contribution without added preparations.
cards.quote: Because this rests on adding prepared vesicles, count it as supported rather than closed.
cards.section: Where the evidence is good, and where it is argued

cards.front: In a mouse prostate-cancer model, deleting Rab27a sharply reduced exosome release and stopped tumour growth in immunocompetent mice, while tumours still grew in immunodeficient mice. What alternative explanation did tumour growth in immunodeficient mice rule out?
cards.back: It ruled out that deleting Rab27a directly crippled tumour-cell proliferation; the growth block required a working immune system.
cards.quote: It ruled out that deleting Rab27a simply crippled tumour-cell proliferation directly; the growth block required a working immune system
cards.section: Where the evidence is good, and where it is argued

cards.front: How did electron microscopy of rat reticulocytes treated with gold-coupled transferrin reveal the exosome release route?
cards.back: Gold-labelled transferrin entered endosomes, appeared on roughly 50 nanometre internal vesicles inside multivesicular compartments, and then appeared on those small vesicles outside cells where compartments fused with the plasma membrane.
cards.quote: Some of these compartments appeared to have fused with the plasma membrane, and their small vesicles were outside the cell.
cards.section: How the route was found

cards.front: Why can you not assume that every cell type uses ESCRT or Rab27a/b in the same way to make and release exosomes?
cards.back: Machinery varies by cell type—for example, ceramide (not ESCRT) loaded a myelin protein in a mouse oligodendrocyte line, while Rab27a/b drove docking in HeLa cells—so each finding holds only where measured.
cards.quote: In a mouse oligodendrocyte cell line, loading one myelin protein into the internal vesicles needed the lipid ceramide and not ESCRT.
cards.section: What sets the door

cards.front: How could tumour vesicles act as decoys against antibody drugs such as anti-HER2 or anti-CD20, and what main caveat limits the evidence?
cards.back: Vesicles carrying the drug target can bind therapeutic antibodies before they reach tumour cells, but most decoy experiments were done in culture where the experimenter chooses the dose.
cards.quote: The decoy experiments were done mostly in culture, where the experimenter chooses the dose.
cards.section: Cancer: decoys, a marker in blood, and the Rab27a question

cards.front: In melanoma patients receiving anti-PD-1 therapy, a larger early rise in PD-L1 on circulating vesicles separated responders from non-responders. Why does this blood correlation not prove that vesicle PD-L1 alters treatment response?
cards.back: By the correlation-versus-causation rule for blood biomarkers, the early rise cannot show whether vesicle PD-L1 changes the response or merely reflects tumour burden or the tumour responding to reactivated T cells.
cards.quote: A correlation in blood cannot show whether vesicle PD-L1 alters the response or reflects the amount of tumour
cards.section: Cancer: decoys, a marker in blood, and the Rab27a question

cards.front: In the mouse prostate-cancer study, why were deleting PD-L1 itself and injecting exosomal PD-L1 to restore tumour growth needed in addition to deleting Rab27a?
cards.back: By the cargo-specificity control rule, Rab27a has other jobs in secretion besides exosome release, so knocking out Rab27a alone cannot isolate exosomal PD-L1; deleting PD-L1 and rescuing growth with exosomal PD-L1 carries the specific causal proof.
cards.quote: In the prostate cancer study, Rab27a has other jobs in secretion, which is why the PD-L1 deletion and exosomal PD-L1 rescue carry the argument.
cards.section: Cancer: decoys, a marker in blood, and the Rab27a question

cards.front: A group uses an artificial loading protocol to pack gene-silencing RNA into purified vesicles and measures high total RNA in the final sample. What artefact of the loading method could make loading look far more efficient than it is?
cards.back: The loading method can cause the RNA to form aggregates that co-isolate with the vesicles, making apparent loading efficiency look much higher than true lumenal encapsulation.
cards.quote: the method used to load such RNA can form aggregates that make loading look more efficient than it is.
cards.section: Loading vesicles with RNA
